fact: The DHIS2 programme (University of Oslo) reports that, a year after the June 2021 pilot in Moyen-Chari and Batha and following the official national launch of DHIS2 in November 2022, 96.4% of Chad's districts were entering their data directly into DHIS2; no numerator or denominator is given.

The DHIS2 programme states that the Ministry of Public Health and Prevention, through its Direction des Statistiques et du Système d'Information Sanitaire and a national DHIS2 team formed inside the ministry in 2019-2020, runs the implementation of DHIS2 as the health management information system, with HISP Rwanda supporting scale-up and PADS supporting districts.

The DHIS2 programme reports that the ministry planned to buy 1,798 tablets for offline data entry with the DHIS2 Android Capture app because of unstable connectivity in the north, and gives a district figure only; it publishes no share or count of health facilities entering their own reports. The World Bank's Chad digital economy diagnostic states that the Ministry of Health implemented DHIS2, a health management data platform, in July 2021 with the financial support of the Global Fund and the GAVI Alliance, and that the project faces challenges in securing sustainable funding for connectivity, energy, maintenance and investment.

The World Bank's diagnostic states that the Ministry of Public Health and National Solidarity implemented DHIS2 in July 2021 and that the platform is used by several entities within the ministry, with the ministry turning to private hosting for it.

WHO's Chad office reports that during the 2024-2025 biennium its support contributed to the validation of the 2024 statistical yearbook, the updating of the reporting tools and their integration into DHIS2, and the validation of a procedures manual for managing health information; it gives no count of facilities or districts.

WHO's Chad office reports that a national digital health strategy was adopted during the 2024-2025 biennium, with WHO supporting the national strategic plan for digital health, its operational plans and a law on health data protection; the report does not say which systems the plan names.

Gavi's programme audit, on site in August 2024, records that in one district visited the district immunisation officer receives the monthly activity reports of 16 health centres and keys them into DHIS2 himself, and that in N'Djamena Centre district (14 health centres, 7 of them private) entry into DHIS2 is likewise done at the district from the monthly vaccination reports the health centres send.

Gavi's programme audit states that the health ministry (MSPP) began moving data management from the manual DVDMT tool to DHIS2 in 2019, that a note of November 2023 from the ministry's Secretary-General to the provincial health delegates required exclusive use of DHIS2, and that the migration was complete only from January 2024.

The Countdown to 2030 country team states that hospitals, which handle nearly half of deliveries, have reported weakly in recent years because their migration from the old health information system to DHIS2 is very slow and resisted by staff, that support to the hospitals has run since 2022 to complete the migration, and that the hospital reporting forms were revised at the end of 2023, delaying data entry.

The Countdown to 2030 country team reports facility reporting rates above 90% since 2020 and the share of districts whose monthly reports are at least 90% complete over a year rising from 78% in 2019 to 83% in 2023, with 2023 completeness held down by hospitals and by some hard-to-reach districts without internet coverage; it gives no share or count of health centres entering their own reports.

The Countdown to 2030 country team, meeting in April 2024, states that the country began integrating the data of private health facilities into its health information system (DHIS2) the previous December and that the process was still under way; private facilities' data had not been counted in earlier years.

The health ministry's PNDS 4 for 2022-2030, dated November 2022, names DHIS2 in its health information pillar: it sets the target of DHIS2 operational in all health districts by 2030, with districts using it synchronised and in real time rising from a baseline of 82% to 100%, and carries budget-coded actions to sustain DHIS2, extend it to districts left out of the initial plan and to health centres, and make it interoperable with the SIGL and the programme trackers.

PNDS 4 states that the ministry's Direction des Statistiques et du Système d'Information Sanitaire (DSSIS) is charged with running every part of the health information system, from designing the tools to producing the information, and describes DHIS2 as the new computerised system deployed with user training, equipment and a central server.

PNDS 4 states that data are collected daily in health facilities on primary tools (registers and forms) and compiled into monthly activity reports (RMA), refers to the entry of the RMA being decentralised to the health districts, and lists extending DHIS2 to the level of the health centres as an action still to be carried out.

PNDS 4 states that DHIS2 has been operational in all provinces since July 2022 and gives a baseline of 82% of health districts using it synchronised and in real time, without numerator or denominator; it publishes no share or count of health centres entering their own reports.

Moukénet and colleagues (BMC Medical Informatics and Decision Making) state that in Chad HMIS data are collected by health facilities on paper forms, checked by the facility manager and reported to the health district, where the zonal chief or district manager converts the data of health facilities and district hospitals to electronic format in Microsoft Excel and sends them by email or flash key to the provincial delegation and then the ministry; the description is undated and is placed at the article's publication year.

Moukénet and colleagues describe reporting at health-centre level as paper-based throughout, with stock-outs of register books at 37.5% and of HMIS forms at 12.5% of the 16 health centres of Massaguet district during 2018, and recommend moving from paper forms to a web-based HMIS; no health centre is described as entering its own data.

Moukénet and colleagues state that health centres and district hospitals report monthly into the HMIS on paper, and measured reporting completeness of 95.24% (CI 90.83-97.92) in the HMIS data of 14 government-recognised health centres in Massaguet district for January-December 2018, with attendance and malaria cases over-reported against the registers (verification factors 1.41 to 2.86).

Moukénet and colleagues state that HMIS data end at the health ministry's Department of Statistics and Health Information (SDSIS), which verifies their consistency at central level and supervises districts and health centres with the malaria programme and the provincial delegation; the description is undated and is placed at the article's publication year.
